long_payload.item_title: Prepare the Northwind onboarding workshop for every regional facilitation team, including the agenda review, facilitator briefings, accessibility and room access requirements, the shared materials library, the follow-up survey, and the handover notes the Northwind launch coordinators asked for after the qualified opportunity review with Avery Chen and the synthetic review panel, so each later reviewer can check the whole request in one place before deciding
long_payload.item_body:
Synthetic long-payload review fixture for the Northwind onboarding workshop. Confirm the agenda, facilitators, and access requirements from the qualified opportunity before anything is scheduled, and keep every note below attached to the one Current item this handoff creates.

Agenda: open with the Northwind launch goals, walk through the onboarding checklist section by section, reserve a long working session for the regional teams to rehearse their own introductions, and close with a question period that the facilitators record for the follow-up survey.

Facilitators: Avery Chen leads the opening and the closing review; two synthetic co-facilitators cover the regional breakout rooms; each facilitator receives the briefing pack, the attendance list, and the escalation contact at the Northwind launch desk (launch-desk@example.com) one week before the workshop.

Access requirements: step-free routes to every room, captioning for the opening and closing sessions, quiet space near the breakout rooms, printed and large-print copies of the agenda, and a recorded walkthrough of the venue for attendees who cannot visit beforehand.

Materials: keep everything in the shared library under northwind-onboarding-workshop-materials-library-reference-index so the coordinators, facilitators, and later reviewers read the same versions without copying files between teams.

Follow-up: send the survey within two working days, collect the facilitator notes the same week, and add the handover summary to this item so the Northwind launch project can pick it up later through Current's own edit form.

pending_spares.note: Each consuming row has its own undecided approval, printed by urls as spare:<row>. The approval-pending and approval-pending-long-payload fixtures are never decided, so their read-only review matrix (themes, viewports, zoom, keyboard) never consumes them.
pending_spares.reseed: Every pending approval, spares included, stays pending for 900 seconds after seeding. When a pending row's window lapses before its check is done, run reset, up and seed again (about three minutes), then browser-stop and browser-start: reset deletes the database that held the review browser's session, so the old window is signed out. Continue with the new URLs from urls. The labels and recipes stay the same; every URL, approval id and workspace id is new.

automated_only.reason: A workspace module is disabled only by writing its module state, and nothing does that: Core has install, enable and upgrade operations but no disable, and only those and export restore write module state. A reviewer would have to edit the database. The PostgreSQL tests set the state directly and pin that a request made while Current is disabled becomes a local handoff with no effect, restages once Current is back, and leaves the linked projection untouched. The omitted state, which a deployment can reach, has its own runtime recipe.

tests: vitest:modules/leads/web/src/handoff-request-form.test.tsx > keeps one user request key across a lost response and retry
automated_only.reason: A lost response means Core committed the request but the reply never reached the browser. Only a network fault between the two produces that, and the acceptance stack adds no fault proxy; a stopped Core refuses the request before anything commits, which is a different state. The form test pins that a retry reuses the same request key, and the PostgreSQL tests pin that the same key returns the same handoff and that concurrent identical requests run one effect.

automated_only.reason: Core's core.operation.resolve has no page or form, and no token of any kind may carry it, so no normal page, CLI or MCP client calls it; reaching it would mean hand-building a request. The unknown-outcome state itself is seeded (handoff-unresolved and approval-unresolved). The PostgreSQL tests pin each resolution outcome and that Leads picks it up.
